description: Choosing a fair sample: random, systematic, stratified-before-sampling, judgement, opportunity and quota.
content_html:
Why Sampling?

A population is everyone or everything the investigation concerns. But collecting data from every member of a population is often impractical — too expensive, too time-consuming, or simply impossible. Instead, a researcher selects a sample: a manageable subset from which conclusions about the whole population can be drawn.

The quality of those conclusions depends critically on how the sample is selected. A badly chosen sample — one that over-represents some groups and under-represents others — produces biased results. No amount of clever analysis can fix a biased sample. This is why choosing the right sampling method is one of the most important decisions in the planning stage of any investigation.

Before sampling can begin, you need a sample frame: a complete list of everyone in the population. For a school survey, the sample frame might be the roll of all registered students. For a national survey, a sample frame might be the electoral register or postcode address file. The sample frame may not include every member of the population — some individuals are always missed — and this itself can be a source of bias.

Methods That Rely on Judgement or Opportunity

Judgement sampling (also called purposive sampling) is where the researcher deliberately chooses participants they believe are typical. It is fast and avoids obvious outliers, but the researcher’s judgement introduces subjectivity and potential bias. If the researcher’s beliefs about the population are wrong, the sample will be wrong in a systematic way.

Opportunity sampling (also called convenience sampling) means selecting whoever is available. Surveying people who happen to be walking past at a particular time, or asking friends and classmates, are examples. It is the cheapest and fastest method, but it is highly susceptible to bias: the people who are available may systematically differ from the wider population in ways that affect the results.

A sample obtained by opportunity or judgement is not automatically worthless. If you are investigating an exploratory question — trying to identify variables worth studying in more depth — a convenient sample gives a quick first look. In early-stage research, speed can outweigh the need for perfect representativeness.

However, any conclusions drawn from such samples must be clearly caveated: they may not apply to the wider population. The examiner will expect you to state this limitation when evaluating an investigation that used judgement or opportunity sampling.

Random Sampling

In a simple random sample, every member of the population has an equal chance of being included, and selections are made using a genuinely random process. This is the gold standard for avoiding systematic bias: no group is systematically favoured or excluded.

Random selection can be achieved using various techniques, including: assigning numbers to all members of the sample frame and using a random number generator, shuffling a pack of cards, or rolling dice. The specification notes these methods but is explicit: you will not be asked to derive a sample using these techniques in the exam — understanding the principle is what matters.

Systematic Sampling

Systematic sampling selects every ‘k’th member of the sample frame after a random start. For example, to select 20 from a list of 200 people, you calculate k = 200 ÷ 20 = 10, choose a random starting point between 1 and 10, then select every 10th person after that.

Systematic sampling is easier to implement than simple random sampling for large populations, and it spreads the sample evenly across the list. However, it can introduce a hidden pattern if the sample frame itself has a regular structure. If a list alternates male/female and you sample every other entry, you might end up with an all-male or all-female sample.

Key Fact

Systematic sampling steps: (1) calculate the sampling interval k = population size ÷ sample size; (2) choose a random start between 1 and k; (3) select every k-th member after that starting point.

Stratification: Not a Sampling Method

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood ideas in the specification. Stratification is a process that happens before sampling — it is not itself a method of sampling. The specification is explicit: stratification is not a method of sampling but a method which may be used before sampling takes place.

Here is how stratification works: first, you divide the population into meaningful subgroups called strata (singular: stratum) based on a characteristic relevant to the investigation. Then, you select participants from each stratum separately, using a random method, in proportion to the size of each stratum in the population.

Example: a school has 300 students: 120 in Year 10 and 180 in Year 11. You want a sample of 50. If you stratify by year group: Year 10 contributes ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​120/300 × 50 = 20 students; Year 11 contributes 180/300 × 50 = 30 students. Within each stratum, you then select randomly. This ensures the sample reflects the year-group balance of the school.

Key Fact

Stratification divides the population into subgroups BEFORE sampling. The actual sampling method used within each stratum is then random sampling. Calling stratification a “sampling method” is a common error that costs marks.

Quota Sampling (Higher)

Quota sampling looks similar to stratification on the surface: you set a target for each subgroup. But there is a crucial difference. In stratified random sampling, participants within each stratum are chosen randomly. In quota sampling, the researcher fills each quota using whoever is available — there is no random selection within the quota. A market researcher might be told to interview 30 women aged 18–25 and 30 women aged 26–40, but they then choose those 60 participants by opportunity — approaching people in a shopping centre until the quotas are met.

Quota sampling is fast and proportional to the population structure, which is why commercial market research firms often use it. However, because selection within each quota is not random, it is susceptible to the same biases as opportunity sampling. The people a researcher approaches in a shopping centre on a weekday morning systematically differ from those who are at work.

Every sampling method trades off between cost/speed and bias risk. Understanding these trade-offs is what the specification is really testing:

  • Opportunity: Fast, cheap, highly biased. Useful only for pilot/exploratory work.
  • Judgement: Fast, avoids obvious outliers, still subjective. Researcher’s assumptions must be sound.
  • Random: Unbiased in expectation, but requires a complete sample frame and may still miss subgroups by chance in small samples.
  • Systematic: Practical for large populations; watch for hidden patterns in the list.
  • Stratification then random: Best for populations with important subgroups — guarantees proportional representation.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about sampling is calling stratification a sampling method. It is not — it is a pre-sampling division of the population. The sampling happens afterwards, within each stratum, using a random method. If a question asks you to compare two sampling methods, state a numerical comparison where possible (e.g. what proportion of each subgroup would be selected) rather than just describing the method in general terms. On ‘Explain’ questions about bias, name the specific group that would be over- or under-represented, not just “the sample might be biased”.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Opportunity sampling is fast but biased; random sampling is the least biased but requires a complete sample frame; systematic sampling is practical for large populations but can be distorted by patterns in the list.
  • Stratification is a division of the population into subgroups that happens before sampling — it is not itself a sampling method. After stratification, random sampling is applied within each stratum to ensure proportional representation.
  • Every sampling decision is a trade-off between bias and practicality — the exam expects you to explain both what a method does and what its specific bias risks are in context.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes stratification in a statistical investigation?
A) Selecting every fifth person from the sample frame.
B) Choosing participants based on who is most convenient to access.
C) Dividing the population into subgroups before sampling takes place.
D) Setting a quota for each subgroup and filling it using random selection.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — Stratification is the division of the population into subgroups (strata) before sampling, not itself a sampling method.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher wants to select a systematic sample of 40 students from a school roll of 400.
Work out the sampling interval and describe how she should select the first member of the sample.
practice_questions.marks:
Sampling interval k = 400 ÷ 40 = 10 [1 mark].
The first member is chosen randomly from members 1 to 10 (e.g. by generating a random number between 1 and 10) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A school wants to investigate students’ attitudes to homework. There are 180 students in Year 10 and 120 students in Year 11. A stratified sample of 30 students is to be taken.
Calculate the number of Year 10 students and Year 11 students that should be included in the sample.
practice_questions.marks:
Total population = 180 + 120 = 300 [1 mark].
Year 10: 180/300 × 30 = 18 students [1 mark].
Year 11: 120/300 × 30 = 12 students [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why opportunity sampling is considered less reliable than simple random sampling for estimating the average income of adults in a city. Refer to a specific group that might be over- or under-represented.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct issues developed with reference to a specific group.
- Opportunity sampling selects whoever is easiest to reach [1] — for example, surveying people outside a city centre shopping area on a weekday morning would over-represent people who are not in paid employment (e.g. retirees, carers, the unemployed), who may have systematically lower incomes than those at work [1].
- By contrast, simple random sampling gives every adult in the city an equal chance of selection [1], so the sample is not systematically skewed towards any income group [1].
Secure: One issue identified with a specific group named.
Developing: Names the sampling method limitations without a specific group.
Emerging: States 'it is biased' without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
A market research company wants to investigate the TV viewing habits of UK adults. They plan to use opportunity sampling at two shopping centres in Manchester on a Saturday afternoon.
Suggest and justify two improvements to this sampling method that would give a more representative sample of all UK adults.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per improvement and 1 mark per justification that links to a specific representativeness issue, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two improvements, each with a justification referencing who is currently under-represented.
- Collect data from multiple locations across the UK, not just Manchester [1], because residents of one city may differ in viewing habits from those in rural areas or other regions, so the current method under-represents non-urban adults [1].
- Collect data at multiple times of day on different days of the week [1], because people who visit shopping centres on Saturday afternoons may differ from those who work weekends or do not go shopping (e.g. those with disabilities or caring responsibilities), systematically excluding groups with different viewing habits [1].
- Switch to a random or stratified method by obtaining a sample frame (e.g. postcodes) and selecting randomly [1], to give every adult an equal chance of selection and remove the geographic and temporal biases of the current approach [1].
Secure: Two improvements, one justified.
Developing: One improvement with a justification.
Emerging: Describes a change without justifying it.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether stratification before sampling is always preferable to simple random sampling. In your answer, give examples of when each method would be most appropriate.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion with examples and a judgement.
Mastering: Advantages of stratification, advantages of simple random sampling, a comparison of when each applies, and a concluding judgement.
- Stratification advantage: guarantees that key subgroups are proportionally represented — for example, if investigating differences in wellbeing between Year 10 and Year 11 students, stratification ensures both year groups appear in the sample in the right proportions [1+1].
- Stratification disadvantage: requires knowledge of the population’s subgroup structure before sampling; if the researcher does not know the relevant groupings in advance, stratification cannot be applied [1+1].
- Simple random sampling advantage: requires only a complete sample frame and no prior knowledge of subgroups; for homogeneous populations (where subgroups are not relevant), it is just as effective and simpler to implement [1+1].
- Judgement: stratification is preferable when the population has known, relevant subgroups and you want guaranteed representation; simple random sampling is preferable for homogeneous populations or when subgroup structure is unknown [1].
Secure: Two threads addressed with partial development.
Developing: One thread with a relevant example.
Emerging: Describes the methods without comparing them.

options: The process of dividing a population into subgroups before sampling
The complete list of every member of the population from which a sample can be drawn
The number of people selected in a stratified sample from each stratum
The method used to collect data from each selected participant

knowledge_checks.q: Which statement about stratification is correct?
options: Stratification is a sampling method used to select participants at random
Stratification is used after sampling to group results
Stratification is a method used before sampling to divide the population into subgroups
Stratification is another term for systematic sampling

knowledge_checks.q: In systematic sampling, the researcher selects every k-th member after a _____ starting point.
Selecting participants simply because they are easy to access, with no randomisation, is called _____ sampling.
Match each sampling method to its key characteristic:
right: Every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
Members are selected at regular intervals after a random start
The researcher deliberately selects participants they believe are representative

flashcard_questions.a: A complete list of every member of the population from which a sample is drawn.
No. Stratification divides the population into subgroups before sampling takes place.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key feature of a simple random sample?
flashcard_questions.a: Every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.

flashcard_questions.q: How is the sampling interval calculated in systematic sampling?
flashcard_questions.a: Sampling interval = population size divided by required sample size.

flashcard_questions.q: What bias risk does opportunity sampling carry?
flashcard_questions.a: Those available to sample may differ systematically from the wider population.

flashcard_questions.q: A school has 200 Year 10 and 100 Year 11 students. A stratified sample of 30 is needed. How many come from Year 11?

flashcard_questions.a: The researcher uses their own judgement to select participants they believe are representative.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between stratification and quota sampling? (Higher)
flashcard_questions.a: Stratification uses random selection within each stratum; quota sampling fills each quota by convenience.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one potential weakness of systematic sampling?
flashcard_questions.a: If the sample frame has a repeating pattern, the regular interval may introduce bias.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might an investigator choose to stratify a population before sampling?
flashcard_questions.a: To guarantee that important subgroups are represented proportionally in the sample.

glossary_terms.definition: The complete set of all individuals or items the investigation is about.
A subset of the population selected for data collection, from which conclusions about the whole population are drawn.
A complete list of every member of the population from which a sample can be drawn.
Sampling where the researcher uses their own judgement to select participants they believe are representative of the population.
Sampling where participants are chosen simply because they are convenient or easy to access, without any randomisation.
A sampling method where every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, and selections are made by a random process.
A sampling method where members are selected from the sample frame at regular intervals, after a random starting point.
Dividing a population into distinct subgroups (strata) based on a shared characteristic, before sampling takes place.
A sampling method where the researcher sets a target number (quota) for each subgroup and then fills each quota using any convenient means.
